# The represented order is not the storage order

This lesson develops A--C. Problem D is explained only in the editorial.

# Problem A: implicit treap sequence surgery

An implicit treap is a randomized BST whose key is the in-order position, recovered from left-subtree sizes. `split(root,k)` returns the first `k` elements and the remainder; `merge(a,b)` requires every element of `a` to precede every element of `b`. Cut/paste becomes a constant number of splits and merges. Random priorities give expected logarithmic height.

# Problem B: lazy sequence aggregates

Store subtree size and sum. Reversal swaps children and toggles a lazy flag; range addition changes the node value, subtree sum, and pending addition. Push tags before using children and pull aggregates after structural changes. The state boundary is exact: every delayed operation affects a whole represented interval.

# Problem C: link-cut trees

A link-cut tree stores each preferred path as an auxiliary splay tree. `access(v)` repeatedly cuts and replaces right preferred children until the root-to-v path is exposed. `makeroot(v)` exposes that path and reverses it, changing the represented-tree root. Then `makeroot(u); access(v)` makes one auxiliary tree represent exactly the u-v path.

The subtle distinction is between an auxiliary-tree root and a represented-tree root. Rotations change only the former. `link` and `cut` change represented edges.

# Split and merge trace

For sequence `ABCDE`, `split(root,2)` returns `AB` and `CDE`. To move `BC` to
the end, split into `A | BC | DE`, then merge `A`, `DE`, and `BC` in that order.
No stored key is updated: subtree sizes reconstruct positions after every
rotation and merge.

The precondition of `merge(left,right)` is semantic—every represented element
of `left` precedes every element of `right`. Random priority chooses the storage
root, but may never reorder the represented sequence.

# Lazy-tag chronology

If a range is first multiplied by `a` and then increased by `b`, its pending
affine tag is `x -> a*x+b`. A later tag `x -> c*x+d` composes outside it:
`x -> c*(a*x+b)+d`. Reversal is structural: swap children and forward/reverse
aggregates, then toggle the flag. Push reversal before relying on which child
is left or right.

# Link-cut exposure trace

After `makeroot(u); access(v)`, the auxiliary splay rooted at `v` contains the
represented path `u..v` in order. A path aggregate is therefore the splay
aggregate at `v`. This statement is true only after both operations; reading a
random auxiliary subtree confuses preferred-path storage with represented-tree
topology.

Before `link(u,v)`, verify they are in different represented trees. To cut an
edge, expose `u..v` and verify that `u` is the direct left child boundary of
`v` with no intervening vertex. Rotations alone never add or remove a
represented edge.

# Implementation and stress testing

Treap code must push before split/merge recursion and pull afterward. Use a
deterministic seeded RNG for reproducible failures. In Python, array-based
nodes reduce memory overhead; iterative alternatives are harder because split
and merge naturally follow tree recursion.

Link-cut correctness depends on `is_aux_root`: a node is an auxiliary root
when its parent does not point to it as a splay child. Push all ancestors before
splaying. Tiny forest oracles can rebuild paths with BFS after every link or
cut and compare aggregates literally.

# Exercises

A--C develop sequence surgery, lazy tags, and exposed forest paths. D is the reconstruction-tree transfer problem.
